description: Reader-facing micro-wiki for historical people, events and factions referenced by Musashi. Novel evidence is spoiler-gated and originates only from the Internet Archive transcription; external sources may be attached separately for modern historical context.

primary_text_source.rule: The novel itself is the only source for claims about what Yoshikawa's narrative says, when an entity appears, how the entity is described in the novel, and relationships revealed by the novel. External sources must never be used to manufacture novel evidence.

novel.evidence: Section 1 explicitly discusses Kobayakawa in connection with the battle and Takezo/Matahachi's aftermath.

context.summary: Daimyō associated with the Western Army at Sekigahara who defected and attacked Ōtani Yoshitsugu's forces, contributing to the Eastern Army victory.

novel.evidence: Section 1 identifies Ishida among the commanders and describes the post-battle military situation.

novel.evidence: Section 1 places the historical commanders of Sekigahara in the narrative's battlefield context.

novel.evidence: Section 1 references the historical commanders involved in the battle.

novel.role: opening historical event and narrative anchor
novel.evidence: Book I opens in the immediate aftermath of Sekigahara, with Takezo and Matahachi among the defeated army.

context.summary: Decisive battle between the Eastern coalition led by Tokugawa Ieyasu and the Western coalition associated with the Toyotomi cause.
Coalition led by Tokugawa Ieyasu during the Sekigahara campaign.
Coalition formed around the Toyotomi cause and opposed the Tokugawa-led Eastern Army at Sekigahara.

novel.role: Zen monk, teacher and major agent in Takezo's transformation
novel.evidence: Section 3 gives substantial narrative biography: birth in Tajima, early religious training, Rinzai affiliation, study with named teachers, residence at Nansōji, appointment as abbot of Daitokuji, and his decision to leave. Later sections establish his role in capturing, confronting and transforming Takezo.

context.summary: Historical Zen monk whose real-life identity is used by Yoshikawa as a major character in the novel. Detailed historical context should remain a separate, spoiler-safe layer.

novel.role: lord of Himeji and authority involved in Takezo's punishment and later release
novel.evidence: The Book I narrative identifies the House of Ikeda in the punishment arrangement and later has Takezo brought before Lord Ikeda Terumasa at Himeji Castle. Terumasa keeps Takezo confined for three years, later offers him service, gives him the name Miyamoto, and permits him to leave.

context.summary: Historical daimyō associated with Himeji. The companion should show historical context separately from Yoshikawa's characterization.

novel.role: political authority governing the Himeji domain in the narrative
novel.evidence: The narrative explicitly refers to the representative of the House of Ikeda in the arrangement surrounding Takezo's capture and punishment.

context.summary: Historical ruling house associated with Himeji in the period relevant to the novel.

novel.role: historical/geographical context referenced around Miyamoto and Mimasaka
novel.evidence: The primary-text audit identifies Akamatsu as a historical-context candidate in the Book I material; this entry remains deliberately minimal until the exact narrative references are audited against the transcription.
